title: Computed Tomography-Based Body Composition Metrics as a Predictor of Textbook Outcome in Lung Transplant Patients.
abstract: Background Lung transplantation is a complex therapy for end stage lung disease with variable postoperative outcomes. Textbook outcomes, defined by freedom from perioperative morbidity and mortality, have emerged as a comprehensive measure of surgical success. Body mass index (BMI) is commonly used to assess nutritional status but does not distinguish between skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. CT-based body composition analysis can differentiate these tissues and may provide a more precise assessment of physiologic reserve in lung transplantation. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of 377 adults undergoing single or bilateral lung transplantation at a single academic institution (2019-2023). Preoperative abdominal CT scans were used to quantify skeletal muscle, subcutaneous fat, and visceral fat areas. A composite textbook outcome was defined as freedom from intraoperative complications; postoperative reintervention; readmission, acute rejection, and dialysis within 30 days; 90-day mortality; primary graft dysfunction; ECMO at 72 h; tracheostomy within 7 days; reintubation; and extubation >48 h. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations between body composition metrics and lung transplant outcomes after adjusting for potential confounders. Results Among 377 recipients, 108 (28.6%) achieved textbook outcome. Increased skeletal muscle area was associated with increased odds of achieving textbook outcome (OR per 50cm 2 : 1.808 [1.061-3.119]) and decreased odds of 1-year mortality (OR per 50cm 2 : 0.423 [0.195-0.890]). Subcutaneous fat area, visceral fat area, and BMI were not significantly associated with outcomes. Conclusion CT-based skeletal muscle was associated with textbook outcome and 1-year mortality, whereas BMI was not. CT-based body composition analysis may be a promising tool for lung transplant risk stratification.

title: Ultrasound-Derived Differential Renal Volume Indexed to Recipient Body Mass Index Predicts One-Year Kidney Graft Function: A Novel Surrogate of Graft-Recipient Size Matching.
abstract: Background Appropriate matching between donor nephron mass and recipient metabolic demand is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of kidney graft outcomes. However, practical and widely applicable methods for estimating graft-recipient size matching remain limited. We investigated whether renal parenchymal volume measured by routine ultrasonography and normalized to recipient body mass index (BMI) is associated with kidney graft function one year after transplantation. Methods In this prospective single-center study, adult kidney transplant recipients underwent routine ultrasonographic assessment one month after transplantation. Renal volumetric parameters, including total renal volume (TRV) and differential renal volume (DRV), were calculated and normalized to recipient BMI. Associations with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at one year were evaluated using correlation and multivariable linear regression analyses adjusted for relevant donor and recipient characteristics. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to assess the discriminatory ability of the most informative volumetric index. Results Renal volumetric parameters were significantly associated with one-year graft function, with stronger associations observed after normalization for recipient BMI. Among the evaluated indices, the DRV/BMI ratio showed the strongest correlation with eGFR and remained independently associated with one-year graft function after multivariable adjustment. Exclusion of renal sinus volume improved the predictive performance of volumetric assessment, supporting the relevance of functional renal parenchyma over total kidney volume. In exploratory ROC analysis, the DRV/BMI ratio demonstrated good discrimination for preserved graft function (AUC 0.774), although the identified threshold requires external validation. Conclusions Ultrasound-derived donor renal parenchymal volume indexed to recipient BMI represents a simple, non-invasive, and clinically applicable surrogate of graft-recipient size matching. If validated in larger multicenter cohorts, this approach may complement existing clinical parameters for predicting graft function and support more individualized post-transplant management.

title: Hemodynamic Analysis of Modified Splenic Arteriovenous Shunt in Pancreas Transplantation.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a modified splenic arteriovenous shunt technique in pancreas transplantation through intraoperative hemodynamic monitoring and postoperative follow-up. Methods A total of 12 patients undergoing simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplantation were enrolled. Under three consecutive intraoperative states (spleen preserved, splenic arteriovenous clamped, and splenic arteriovenous shunt created), color Doppler ultrasound was used to measure peak systolic velocity (PS) and volumetric flow (VF) of the splenic artery and vein at the same point in the distal pancreatic tail, while portal venous pressure was recorded using an intravascular pressure transducer. Postoperative graft function, thrombotic events, and complications were regularly followed up. Results Compared with the spleen-preserved state, the clamped state showed significant reductions in splenic arterial PS and VF (15.24 ± 4.43 cm/s, 16.62 ± 6.84 mL/min) and splenic venous PS and VF (16.31 ± 3.82 cm/s, 60.32 ± 16.07 mL/min) (P < 0.001). In the shunt state, splenic arterial (54.47 ± 3.45 cm/s, 157.39 ± 11.24 mL/min) and venous (49.27 ± 6.61 cm/s, 177.89 ± 14.15 mL/min) flow parameters showed no significant differences compared with the spleen-preserved state (P > 0.05), but were significantly higher than those in the clamped state (P < 0.001). Portal venous pressure showed no significant differences among the three states (P > 0.05). At a median follow-up of 5 months, no graft thrombosis, pancreatitis, or gastrointestinal bleeding was observed, and patient and graft survival rates were both 100% at the last follow-up. Glycated hemoglobin decreased from 7.37% ± 0.68% preoperatively to 5.81% ± 0.32% (P < 0.005), and left ventricular ejection fraction increased from 59.50% ± 3.23% to 67.33% ± 2.84% (P < 0.005). Conclusion The modified splenic arteriovenous shunt maintains physiological perfusion of the pancreatic allograft without elevating portal venous pressure, and may mitigate the hypoperfusion and blood stasis associated with conventional splenic vessel ligation. Based on the short-term results of this study, this modified technique appears safe and feasible, and may contribute to reducing early thrombotic complications after pancreas transplantation.

title: PRAME Immunohistochemistry and Molecular Profiling in Undifferentiated Cutaneous Pleomorphic Neoplasms: A Case Series of 8 Tumors.
abstract: Background Undifferentiated cutaneous pleomorphic neoplasms are diagnostically challenging, as histopathology and immunohistochemistry often fail to identify undifferentiated melanoma in lesions that instead remain classified provisionally as atypical fibroxanthoma (AFX) or pleomorphic dermal sarcoma (PDS). Given the prognostic and therapeutic implications of melanoma, additional ancillary tools may be helpful in selected cases. Methods We studied eight patients with undifferentiated pleomorphic neoplasms using molecular profiling and PRAME immunohistochemistry, correlating findings with clinical behavior. Results Molecular findings varied across the cohort. Two tumors harbored NRAS hotspot mutations and were associated with aggressive clinical courses. In one patient, the tumor showed focal melanoma in situ associated with an undifferentiated intradermal tumor harboring NF1, TERT, and TP53 variants. The remaining tumors lacked melanoma-associated hotspot mutations. Diffuse PRAME expression was seen in three patients with an established diagnosis of melanoma and three patients with AFX/PDS. Two patients with AFX/PDS were negative for PRAME expression. Conclusions Molecular profiling may provide supportive diagnostic evidence for melanoma lineage in a subset of undifferentiated cutaneous pleomorphic neoplasms when interpreted in conjunction with morphology, immunohistochemistry, and clinical findings. In contrast, diffuse PRAME expression was observed in a nonspecific fashion both in cases with melanoma driver mutations and molecularly nonspecific cases in this cohort, limiting its utility as a standalone screening test for triaging molecular analysis.

title: Cytomorphologic Features of Hepatic PEComa Diagnosed by Fine-Needle Aspiration Biopsy.
abstract: Perivascular epithelioid cell tumours (PEComas) are rare mesenchymal neoplasms with characteristic myomelanocytic differentiation and limited descriptions in fine-needle aspiration (FNA) specimens. A woman in her 30s with a history of ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma in remission was found to have a 2.1-cm hepatic mass during evaluation of persistent liver function abnormalities. Ultrasound-guided FNA demonstrated a cellular neoplasm composed of loosely cohesive clusters and singly dispersed epithelioid to spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, mild to moderate nuclear atypia and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical studies showed positivity for smooth muscle actin, caldesmon, HMB-45 and Melan-A, supporting a myomelanocytic phenotype. Molecular testing identified pathogenic TSC2 splice-site mutations. Subsequent resection confirmed hepatic PEComa, epithelioid angiomyolipoma variant. This case highlights the characteristic cytomorphologic, immunophenotypic and molecular features of hepatic PEComa and demonstrates the value of FNA with ancillary testing in establishing a preoperative diagnosis and excluding morphologic mimics.

title: Unravelling A Rare Diagnosis: Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis.
abstract: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) is a rare disorder characterized by abnormal accumulation of surfactant within the alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange and progressive respiratory symptoms. We report a 40-year-old stone grinder presenting with chronic cough, dyspnea, weight loss and hypoxemia. High-resolution computed tomography showed bilateral ground-glass opacities, while bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) yielded characteristic milky fluid. Cytological examination demonstrated PAS-positive eosinophilic material with foamy macrophages, confirming secondary PAP related to silica exposure. Lung biopsy was not feasible because of the patient's condition. Whole lung lavage resulted in marked clinical, radiological and oxygenation improvement, highlighting BAL cytology's diagnostic value.

title: EUS Shear Wave Elastography for Assessing Pancreatic Fibrosis: An Exploratory Study of Its Histological Correlation.
abstract: Objectives Endoscopic ultrasound shear wave elastography (EUS-SWE) enables quantitative, noninvasive assessment of tissue elasticity. However, the association between EUS-SWE and pancreatic histology remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the utility of EUS-SWE for predicting pancreatic fibrosis by comparing it with histological findings of resected specimens. Methods Patients who underwent EUS-SWE before pancreatectomy between October 2019 and October 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. SWE was performed near the surgical resection margin, and shear wave velocity (Vs, m/s) was measured. The number of EUS morphological findings according to the Rosemont classification was obtained. Histological findings were assessed using quantitative analysis and grading analysis. The association between EUS-SWE or the number of EUS morphological findings and histological findings, as well as the diagnostic performance of EUS-SWE and EUS morphological findings for predicting histological fibrosis at predefined fibrosis thresholds (≥ 5%, ≥ 10%, ≥ 15%, and ≥ 20%) was evaluated. Results Thirty-four patients were included. Vs correlated significantly with quantitative fibrosis (ρ = 0.73, p < 0.001), but not with fatty infiltration and inflammation. The number of EUS morphological findings correlated only with fibrosis grade (ρ = 0.35, p = 0.041). EUS-SWE had higher diagnostic accuracy than EUS morphological findings for predicting histological fibrosis at all thresholds (91.2%, 88.2%, 82.4%, and 88.2% vs. 55.9%, 67.6%, 55.9%, and 50.0%, respectively). Conclusions EUS-SWE may serve as a quantitative, noninvasive method for evaluating pancreatic fibrosis. Trial registration UMIN ID: 000058397.

title: Ηip dysplasia in children with spina bifida after prenatal surgical closure.
abstract: Aim To determine the prevalence of neonatal hip dysplasia in children with spina bifida after prenatal surgical closure and examine its association with functional level and preterm birth. Method We conducted a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected standardized registry data from a tertiary specialized centre providing comprehensive spina bifida diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. Standardized hip ultrasound according to the Graf method was performed as part of a protocolized clinical pathway after prenatal surgery, within the first week of life corrected for preterm birth. The primary outcome was the prevalence of hip dysplasia at the initial ultrasound. Associations between hip status, functional level, and gestational age were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation. Results A total of 212 children (101 males, 111 females) underwent prenatal surgical closure between 1st January 2011 and 30th August 2022; 168 children (336 hips) had available neonatal ultrasound data and were included in the analysis. Preterm birth was present in 138 (82%) of 168 children, including 99 (59%) born late preterm, 35 (21%) born very preterm, and four (2%) born extremely preterm. At the initial ultrasound, 286 (85%) of 336 hips were mature, 33 (9.8%) were immature, and 17 (5.1%) were dysplastic. Worse hip status was weakly associated with a higher functional level (r = -0.243; p < 0.001), whereas no significant association was found between hip dysplasia and preterm birth (p = 0.080). Interpretation The prevalence of neonatal hip dysplasia in children with spina bifida after prenatal surgical closure was within the range reported for the general population.

title: Imaging the Adult With Secundum Atrial Septal Defect: A Practical Echocardiographic Approach From Diagnosis to Device Closure.
abstract: Background Secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) is one of the most common congenital heart defects encountered in adults. Echocardiography plays a central role in diagnosis, assessment of haemodynamic significance, anatomical characterization, transcatheter closure planning, and follow-up. However, the frequently non-circular geometry of secundum ASD can make accurate anatomical assessment challenging, particularly with single-plane measurements. Purpose This narrative review provides a practical echocardiographic approach to adult secundum ASD, emphasizing the complementary roles of transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), multiplanar two-dimensional transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), color Doppler, and three-dimensional (3D) TEE. Content TTE provides initial diagnosis and assessment of physiological consequences, including right-sided chamber remodeling, ventricular function, tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary pressure. Multiplanar 2D TEE enables systematic assessment of ASD size, morphology, and surrounding septal rims, while measurements obtained in different planes may reveal substantial differences and highlight the limitations of single-plane sizing. 3D TEE provides an en-face spatial representation of the interatrial septum and complements 2D measurements by defining defect geometry, rim relationships, and suitability for transcatheter closure. Haemodynamic assessment should integrate right ventricular volume overload, shunt magnitude, pulmonary vascular status, and left ventricular disease rather than defect diameter alone. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance or cardiac computed tomography may provide complementary information when echocardiography is insufficient to define pulmonary venous connections, anatomy, or haemodynamics. Conclusion A systematic multimodality echocardiographic approach integrates anatomical and physiological information throughout the management of adult secundum ASD. Combining TTE, multiplanar 2D TEE, 3D TEE, and targeted advanced imaging can facilitate individualized assessment and informed transcatheter closure planning.

title: Not Only the Left Ventricle: The Impact of Potentially Cardiotoxic Oncological Treatment on the Left Atrium and Right Ventricle.
abstract: Background Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and global longitudinal strain (GLS) remain recommended for cardiotoxicity surveillance during cancer therapy, yet it changes late and overlooks injury to the other cardiac chambers. Purpose We systematically reviewed echocardiographic and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) studies that assessed left atrial (LA), right atrial (RA), and right ventricular (RV) function in patients exposed to potentially cardiotoxic oncological treatment. Methods PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched for English-language studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, following the PRISMA recommendations. Across tumor types-lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, breast, gastrointestinal, and melanoma-and across anthracycline-, trastuzumab-, fluoropyrimidine-, and immune checkpoint inhibitor-based regimens, strain imaging detected subclinical dysfunction that conventional measures missed. Results LA reservoir strain declined early and frequently preceded any fall in LVEF, outperforming volumetric LA indices for the detection and prediction of cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD). RV deformation parameters, particularly free-wall longitudinal strain and three-dimensional RV ejection fraction, identified RV involvement that was sometimes independent of LV cardiotoxicity and was associated with adverse cardiac events. Data on the RA remain sparse but point in the same direction. Conclusion Multichamber strain assessment adds sensitivity to LVEF and GLS-based monitoring; standardization of acquisition, reference values, and reporting is needed before it can enter routine cardio-oncology surveillance.

title: Structural Brain Correlates of Digit-Span Performance in Adults: A Narrative Review of Evidence From Lesion and MRI Studies.
abstract: The digit-span task is a widely used measure of working memory in clinical and research contexts. Although numerous studies have examined its neuroanatomical correlates, research findings are heterogeneous, and a clear synthesis of structural evidence is warranted. This review aimed to synthesise existing evidence linking structural integrity of brain regions (volume or lesion) with digit-span performance in adults, using findings from 23 peer-reviewed studies. Functional imaging studies, composite digit-span scores and paediatric/adolescent samples were excluded. PubMed search supplemented by citation tracking identified 23 eligible studies (17 lesion and six structural MRI) published until December 2025. Six regions were related to both forward and backward digit-span task performance (left inferior parietal, left insula, bilateral supplementary motor, bilateral cerebellum, left middle temporal and left thalamus regions). Forward span was uniquely associated with six left-hemisphere regions including the left superior temporal, caudate, putamen, superior frontal, inferior temporal and precuneus. Backward span was uniquely associated with the bilateral superior parietal, bilateral hippocampus, left sensorimotor, right precuneus and right posterior cingulate regions. Dorsolateral prefrontal and inferior frontal findings were mixed. Partially distinct neuroanatomical profiles between forward and backward digit-span tasks likely reflect differences between attentional control/storage demands and higher executive/manipulation demands, respectively. In conclusion, digit-span performance is related to a distributed neural network spanning cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions. While forward and backward digit-span tasks share common substrates, distinct regions are also recruited, consistent with differing cognitive demands. These findings may inform clinical interpretation and targeted cognitive interventions for prevention and rehabilitation of working memory deficits.

title: Impact of a Specialized Care Pathway for ICU Patients With Disorders of Consciousness: Observational Insights From an Expert Center.
abstract: Background Management of lasting disorders of consciousness (DoC) is complex and sometimes requires referral of patients to an expert team. We aimed to evaluate the impact of such specialized expert assessment through the description of a single-center experience. Method Monocentric study including all patients with DoC referred to a tertiary neuroICU for multimodal clinical, electrophysiological, and MRI assessment allowing diagnostic and therapeutic proposals and multidisciplinary prognostic prediction. The primary endpoint was the patients' actual outcome, assessed by 3-month functional disability and 1-year mortality, according to the predicted prognosis. Results Between July 2017 to June 2024, 124 patients (median age 61 [49-70] years, 67% of men) were referred from 43 departments of 37 primary hospitals. Most frequent etiologies were post-anoxic encephalopathy (62%) and secondary systemic brain injuries (15%). At a median of 23 [15-33] days after DoC onset, predicted prognosis was good in 20 (16%) patients, intermediate in 41 (33%), and poor in 63 (51%). Three-month GOS-E was 3 [1-3], 2 [1-3], and 1 [1] (p < 0.001) and 1-year mortality was 30%, 41%, and 82% (p < 0.001), respectively. Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies increased with worsening predicted prognosis (38%, 41%, and 65%, respectively, p < 0.001), but functional disability and mortality remained higher in the poor prognosis group (p < 0.003 and p < 0.039, respectively) even after excluding patients with those decisions. Conclusion Specialized consciousness assessment impacts the ethical decisions made by primary centers and helps refine the prediction of recovery but fails to achieve highly accurate individual prediction in a population with overall poor survival and functional prognosis.

title: Serum GFAP and Age Accurately Distinguish AQP4-IgG Positive and Double Seronegative NMOSD From MOGAD After a Recent Attack.
abstract: Background Serum neurofilament-light chain (sNfL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (sGFAP) are associated with multiple sclerosis (MS) activity. This study aimed to identify patient- and disease-level determinants of sNfL and sGFAP and to evaluate their ability to support differential diagnosis in neuromyelitis optica (NMO). Methods sNFL and sGFAP levels were measured in 640 patients from the OFSEP cohort (88 NMO spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies [AQP4-NMOSD], 28 double-seronegative NMOSD [DN-NMOSD], 61 myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease [MOGAD], 64 clinically isolated syndrome [CIS], 237 relapsing-remitting MS [RRMS], and 162 primary progressive MS [PPMS]). The association between log[sNFL] and log[sGFAP] and age, sex, time since relapse, EDSS, oligoclonal bands, and MRI characteristics was analyzed by multiple linear regression. The diagnostic performance of sNfL and sGFAP in discriminating between NMOSD and MS subgroups was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression and area under the curve (AUC). Results For each group, specific associations of sNFL and sGFAP levels with patient characteristics were observed. Clearest associations were observed in AQP4-NMOSD patients. After a recent attack (≤ 90 days), multivariate analysis revealed that sGFAP and age discriminated AQP4-NMOSD from MOGAD (AUC = 0.939 [0.910;0.982]), AQP4-NMOSD and DN-NMOSD from MOGAD (AUC = 0.863 [0.776;0.977]), and AQP4-NMOSD from all other groups (AUC = 0.950 [0.918;0.987]). Diagnostic probability heatmaps based on sGFAP and age illustrate the probability of each diagnosis relative to others for bedside interpretation. Conclusion After an acute attack of NMOSD, risk score based on sGFAP and age may guide the management of patients before autoantibody status is available.

title: Comparison of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease Between Individuals With Werner Syndrome and Those With Insulin-Resistant Type 2 Diabetes: Hepatic Steatosis and Fibrosis Indices.
abstract: Aim This study compared metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) in individuals with Werner syndrome (WS) and individuals with insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes (T2D). It also examined the association with imaging findings of MASLD in individuals with WS, clarified the characteristics of MASLD that accompany WS, and identified useful indices for its diagnosis in addition to imaging. Methods Three hepatic steatosis and two hepatic fibrosis indices in 48 individuals enrolled in the Japanese Werner Syndrome Registry were compared with those in 101 Japanese individuals with insulin-resistant T2D from another clinical study. In individuals with WS, the liver/spleen ratio (L/S ratio) was calculated from computed tomography (CT) images, and its associations with each index were examined. Statistical analyses were performed using the Welch test and pairwise comparisons. Results Individuals with WS had lower hepatic steatosis and fibrosis index values than those with insulin-resistant T2D. The mean L/S ratio calculated from CT images was 1.05 ± 0.24 in individuals with WS. The L/S ratio, which is one of the indicators for diagnosing MASLD, was < 0.9 in 5 of 20 cases (25%). Among the various indices in individuals with WS, only the hepatic steatosis index (HSI) was correlated with the L/S ratio (r = -0.863, p = 0.0003). Conclusions The prevalence of MASLD is lower in individuals with WS than in those with insulin-resistant T2D. The HSI was associated with the L/S ratio in individuals with WS, suggesting that HSI may reflect hepatic steatosis-related changes in this population. Further studies in larger cohorts are needed to validate these findings. title: Gray and white matter structural alterations in migraine with and without aura: A multimodal MRI and JuSpace analysis.
abstract: Objective To characterize gray and white matter structural alterations in migraine without aura (MwoA) and migraine with aura (MwA) relative to healthy controls (HC), test direct differences between the migraine groups, and examine spatial associations between voxel-based morphometry findings and molecular and cellular reference templates. Background Structural and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have reported gray and white matter abnormalities in migraine, but findings vary across cohorts, imaging methods, and clinical subgroups. Whether migraine with and without aura show distinct structural patterns remains uncertain, and the molecular and cellular context of these alterations is incompletely understood. Methods This cross-sectional group-comparison analysis was embedded in an ongoing prospective single-center study at The First Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University in Dalian, China, and included participants recruited from August 2025 to March 2026. Thirty HC, 40 participants with MwoA, and 15 participants with MwA underwent T1-weighted and diffusion MRI. Diffusion tensor imaging, neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging, and diffusional kurtosis imaging metrics were analyzed using tract-based spatial statistics; gray matter microstructure and volume were assessed using gray matter-based spatial statistics and voxel-based morphometry (VBM). JuSpace Toolbox correlated unthresholded VBM statistical parametric t (spmT) maps with neurotransmitter- and cell-related templates. Models adjusted for age, sex, and education; VBM additionally adjusted for total intracranial volume; and direct MwoA-versus-MwA sensitivity models included Patient Health Questionnaire-9. Results Relative to HC, MwoA showed higher mean and radial diffusivity and lower neurite density index, whereas MwA showed lower free-water fraction (all threshold-free cluster enhancement-family-wise error [FWE], p < 0.05). No diffusional kurtosis imaging or corrected gray matter-based spatial statistics result was significant. VBM showed lower gray matter volume in MwoA in left cerebellar Crus I (77 voxels; peak-level whole-brain family-wise error (FWE)-corrected p value (pFWE) = 0.022) and right inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis (6 voxels; pFWE = 0.025), and in MwA in right inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis (85 voxels; pFWE = 0.019). Direct MwoA-versus-MwA comparisons were nonsignificant in primary and Patient Health Questionnaire-9-adjusted models. JuSpace identified seven and 11 false discovery rate (FDR)-significant neurotransmitter-related associations for MwoA-versus-HC and MwA-versus-HC, respectively; no cell-related template survived FDR correction for MwoA-versus-HC, whereas nine survived for MwA-versus-HC (q < 0.05). No region of interest-clinical association survived Bonferroni correction. Conclusion Multimodal MRI identified gray and white matter alterations in both migraine groups relative to HC, whereas direct MwoA-versus-MwA comparisons were nonsignificant. JuSpace provided complementary spatial context for the VBM findings. These results broaden the structural characterization of migraine but do not establish imaging differences between the two migraine groups.

title: Association between bacterial load and volumetric bone loss in teeth with persistent apical periodontitis: A cone-beam computed tomography segmentation-based observational study.
abstract: Aim To quantitatively compare the bacterial DNA load in root apices and periapical lesions surgically retrieved from teeth with failed root canal treatment, and to investigate the association between bacterial DNA load in both anatomical locations and the three-dimensional (3D) volumetric extent of periapical bone loss, as well as relevant clinical and demographic variables. Methodology Root apices and periapical lesions were surgically obtained from patients with failed root canal treatments. Samples were cryopulverized and bacterial DNA was quantified by q-PCR assay. The volume of the periapical lesions was calculated by cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images segmentation using Blue Sky Bio software. Demographic and clinical data including gender, age, previous retreatment, tenderness to percussion, tooth position, and periapical healing after 1 year were preliminarily associated with the lesion volume. Normality of the variables was analyzed by the Shapiro Wilk test, and global comparisons were explored by ANOVA when variances were similar. The Student t test was used for pair-by-pair comparisons. Results Seventy-nine samples (40 root apices and 39 lesions) were successfully amplified. A greater number of DNA copies was found in apices as compared with apical lesions (p < 0.05). Analysis by lesion volume showed that a higher bacterial load in apices was associated with larger apical lesions, as well as in lesions of patients under 50 years old (p < 0.05). Clinical parameters such as tooth position and patient age showed an association with the volume of apical lesions (p < 0.05). Conclusions Root apices harbour higher bacterial DNA than periapical lesions, regardless of the volume of apical bone loss. Apices associated with large volume lesions present a greater amount of bacterial DNA. Preliminary associations were identified between certain clinical and demographic factors (age and tooth position) and increased lesion volume.

title: Three-Dimensional Segmentation of Dens Invaginatus: A Case Series Exploring the CARES Classification for Anatomy-Driven Clinical Decision-Making.
abstract: Introduction Dens invaginatus (DI) exhibits substantial 3-dimensional anatomical variability that may not be fully represented by conventional classification systems. The recently introduced CARES classification provides a CBCT-based framework incorporating communication, cross-sectional anatomy, root formation, vertical extent, and supplementary features. This case series aims to describe the clinical management of three teeth with DI using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and three-dimensional segmentation for anatomical assessment and treatment planning, while illustrating the clinical application of the CARES classification. Methods Three maxillary lateral incisors with DI and periradicular pathosis were evaluated using CBCT and 3-dimensional segmentation of the tooth and root canal system. Anatomical features were categorized according to both Oehlers and CARES classifications. Treatment strategies were individualized according to the anatomical configuration encountered in each case. One tooth was managed using conventional CBCT-assisted access, whereas static guided endodontic access was used in 2 anatomically complex cases following unsuccessful conventional localization of the target anatomy. Results Case 1, classified as Oehlers Type II and CARES C1-A0-R2-E2-S1, presented an invagination communicating with the root canal without displacement or deformation of the canal and was successfully managed using conventional CBCT-assisted access, with complete periradicular healing after 7 years. Cases 2 and 3 were classified as Oehlers Type IIIa and CARES C2-A1-R2-E2-S3 and C2-A1-R2-E2-S2, respectively. In both cases, the invagination communicated with the periodontium but not with the root canal system and displaced or deformed the root canal, resulting in a C-shaped configuration in Case 2 and an asymmetrical, flattened configuration in Case 3. Static guided endodontics enabled access to anatomically challenging targets after conventional approaches proved insufficient. Follow-up demonstrated clinical resolution in all cases, with complete periradicular healing at 7 years in Case 1, progressive periradicular healing at 6 months in Case 2, and significant periradicular healing at 24 months in Case 3. Conclusion CBCT combined with three-dimensional segmentation provided detailed characterization of DI anatomy and supported individualized treatment planning. Application of the CARES classification captured clinically relevant anatomical and disease-related features not conveyed by Oehlers classification alone, particularly communication patterns, root canal deformation, and the origin of periradicular pathosis. These cases illustrate the potential clinical value of integrating three-dimensional anatomical assessment and CARES coding when managing complex DI.

title: Melanoma Prognostication Using AI-Guided Histopathology.
abstract: Accurate diagnosis and risk stratification are central for optimal management of patients with melanoma. Current American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging systems inadequately stratify patients with clinically meaningful metastatic potential. Manual histopathologic interpretation compounds this limitation, particularly for diagnostically ambiguous lesions at the benign-malignant interface, where concordance is highly variable. This review examines how computational pathology and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can improve histopathologic diagnosis and risk stratification of melanoma, evaluate current image-based deep learning (DL) approaches, and outline a path toward explainable, multimodal prognostic tools. We review published DL models applied to hematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images (H&E WSIs) for melanoma diagnosis, subtype classification, and survival prediction, and discuss integration with transcriptomic and spatial proteomic data modalities. Computational pathology, informed by deep learning, can reliably identify melanomas at risk of disease recurrence and progression. These inferences can be enhanced by integration of spatial molecular profiling, which can also provide mechanistic explainability to the H&E-based DL models. However, limitations in dataset diversity, external validation, model interpretability, and generalizability across populations and image acquisition protocols currently prevent clinical adoption. Outcome-anchored, multimodal computational pathology pipelines integrating H&E WSIs with spatial multi-omic profiling offer a biologically grounded and scalable framework for personalized risk stratification in stage I-III CM, with potential to standardize diagnosis, discover novel prognostic features, and inform individualized treatment strategies.

title: Can We Diagnose Early Melanoma by Genomics?
abstract: Melanoma incidence has increased approximately 6-fold over the past 40 years, driven primarily by melanoma in situ and thin invasive melanomas, which are among the most subjective lesions to diagnose on histopathology. This review examines whether genomics clarifies the "gray zone" between benign and malignant pigmented lesions, or instead recasts existing histopathologic ambiguity in molecular terms, while also considering whether genomic classification shifts overdiagnosis upstream instead of resolving underlying diagnostic uncertainty. Across cytogenetic, mutation-based, and gene-expression platforms, current assays perform best in unequivocal melanoma-versus-nevus comparisons and lose accuracy in diagnostically ambiguous lesions where clarification is most needed. Gene expression profile (GEP) tests can be useful diagnostic aids in tissue-rich equivocal lesions, including atypical Spitz tumors, MELTUMPs, and cellular blue nevus/blue nevus-like melanocytoma differentials. One clinicopathologic-genomic model, the Merlin CP-GEP test, has been prospectively validated for predicting sentinel lymph node status and is now recognized as supporting sentinel lymph node biopsy decisions in T1b/T2a melanomas. Importantly, a low-risk prognostic GEP class assignment should not displace the standard sentinel lymph node biopsy discussion. GEP tests are least useful for small, thin, equivocal junctional proliferations, precisely the lesions that are most difficult to diagnose. Pre-biopsy non-invasive assays carry the additional risk of lowering, rather than raising, the biopsy threshold. Overall, current genomic tools should be viewed as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, histopathology and clinical context.

title: Intraoperative Ultrasound Guided Sling Adjustment During Transobturator Sling Placement: A Preliminary Pilot Report of the Technical Protocol and Feasibility.
abstract: Objectives To describe a qualitative intraoperative ultrasound protocol for transobturator mid-urethral sling adjustment and assess technical feasibility. Methods This retrospective pilot series included 58 consecutive women with urodynamically confirmed stress urinary incontinence or stress-predominant mixed urinary incontinence undergoing outside-in transobturator sling placement. Sagittal and axial images guided gentle traction for a visible tape-urethra gap and tension release for urethral encroachment. Sling-arm oscillation supplemented assessment when acoustic shadowing limited visualization. Feasibility measures included visualization, adjustment frequency, final sonographic findings, scanning duration, and intraoperative complications. Clinical outcomes were summarized using available cases. Results The tape was visualized in all 58 procedures and adjusted in 26 (44.8%). No final residual gap or encroachment was observed. Median scanning duration was 3 min 45 s (interquartile range, 3-4 min); no intraoperative complications were recorded. All 58 women provided baseline and 3-month questionnaire data. Mean six-item Urogenital Distress Inventory scores decreased from 68.3 ± 17.2 to 20.0 ± 6.7; seven-item Incontinence Impact Questionnaire scores decreased from 75.4 ± 10.5 to 18.2 ± 6.7. At 36 months, 20/58 women (34.5%) had outcome data. All 20 met the objective stress continence criterion (exact two-sided 95% confidence interval, 83.2%-100%); none met the objective voiding dysfunction criterion (exact two-sided 95% confidence interval, 0%-16.8%). These findings concern only the retained subgroup. Conclusions The protocol was technically feasible in this single-surgeon, single-center series. Reproducibility, workflow burden, and clinical benefit require prospective evaluation.

title: Preprocedural Computed Tomography Guidance Improves Accuracy of Right Ventricular Septal Lead Placement in Pacemaker Implantation.
abstract: Introduction Accurate right ventricular septal lead placement is crucial for optimal pacemaker performance and procedural safety, yet conventional fluoroscopy-guided implantation is limited by inter-individual anatomical variability. We therefore examined whether preprocedural computed tomography (CT) can provide patient-specific anatomical guidance to enable precise lead positioning. Methods and results We retrospectively analyzed 501 consecutive patients who underwent initial dual-chamber pacemaker implantation for bradycardia pacing (non-CT-guided, n = 243; CT-guided, n = 258). In the CT-guided group, the midseptal target was determined preoperatively using multiplanar reconstruction of CT images, and reference lines were projected onto the scout image to guide lead placement. We evaluated the total procedure time, fluoroscopy time, right ventricular lead electrical parameters, implantation site, and complications. CT guidance was associated with a higher rate of septal lead placement than non-CT guidance (93.0% vs. 55.6%, p < 0.001), whereas free-wall lead placement was less frequent (7.0% vs. 44.4%, p < 0.001). The procedural radiation dose was lower with CT guidance (CT-guided, 100.2 ± 124.6 mGy vs. non-CT-guided, 169.1 ± 152.4 mGy; p < 0.001). Among patients with complete atrioventricular block and available postoperative paced QRS measurements (n = 303), QRS duration was shorter in the CT-guided group than in the non-CT-guided group (145.3 ± 22.3 ms [n = 165] vs. 155.4 ± 19.0 ms [n = 138], p < 0.001). The association persisted after multivariable adjustment ((adjusted OR, 10.30; 95% CI, 5.91-17.97; p < 0.001). The total procedure time, fluoroscopy time, and pacing parameters were comparable between the groups. Complication rates were low overall, and pocket hematoma was less frequent in the CT-guided group (0.4% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.03). Conclusion Preprocedural CT guidance facilitated precise planning of the right ventricular lead target using scout images and was associated with accurate and reproducible placement at the intended septal site without prolonging procedural time or compromising electrical performance. This approach may represent a practical strategy for optimizing lead placement in bradycardia pacing.

title: Association Between Local Factors and Implant-Related Complications: A Population-Sampled Cross-Sectional Analysis.
abstract: Aim To investigate the role of local factors and the association with peri-implantitis and peri-implant soft-tissue dehiscence (PISTD). Materials and methods A randomly selected sample of Norwegian patients who underwent implant therapy in 2014 was examined (242 patients; 732 implants). Clinical and radiographic parameters were recorded, including soft-tissue phenotype, mucosal margin mobility, connection type, platform switching, emergence angle, implant location and presence of adjacent teeth. To account for clustering of implants within patients, mixed-effects logistic regression models were applied. Results Mucosal margin mobility, bone-level implants without platform switching, emergence angle > 45°, anterior implant location and daily smoking were identified as significant risk indicators for peri-implantitis. Thin soft-tissue phenotype, mucosal margin mobility, absence of adjacent teeth, peri-implantitis and external connection were detected as significant indicators for PISTD. Peri-implantitis and PISTD were present in 8.7% and 25.0% of implants, respectively. Conclusions Local factors and soft-tissue-related parameters, many modifiable during treatment planning, were associated with peri-implantitis and PISTD. Particular attention should be given to soft-tissue phenotype, connection design, platform switching and prosthetic emergence angle. The relationship between systemic and local risk factors should be further investigated.

title: Influence of the Occupying Proportion of Mineralised Particles Within the Grafted Volume on Subsequent Volume Shrinkage: A Preclinical Study on Rabbit Calvaria.
abstract: Aim To evaluate whether mineral particle occupancy within the grafted volume influences volumetric stability and bone regeneration, and to compare particulate grafts, collagenated grafts, hyaluronic acid-conjugated particulates and mechanical manipulation in a vertical augmentation model. Materials and methods Ten New Zealand white rabbits received four standardised vertical calvarial defects and filled with saline-hydrated particulate deproteinised porcine bone mineral (Control), intact collagenated bone blocks (CBM), hydrated and mechanically crushed collagenated blocks (cCBM) or particulate grafts mixed with hyaluronic acid (HA). Grafts were placed in sealed plastic cylinders. Animals were sacrificed at 2 and 8 weeks. Volumetric stability and mineralised tissue volume were assessed by micro-computed tomography, and the total augmented area, new bone formation, residual material and particle length were evaluated by histological and histomorphometric analyses. Data were analysed using linear mixed-effects models. Results Mineralised tissue volume increased over time in Control, CBM and HA groups but decreased in cCBM (time × material interaction, p = 0.020). At 8 weeks, total augmented area was preserved in Control and CBM, whereas significant volumetric shrinkage occurred in cCBM and HA (p < 0.01). New bone formation increased in all groups but was highest in the Control group. Residual material area remained stable but was higher in Control and CBM than in cCBM and HA, and particle length was reduced in mechanically manipulated groups. Conclusions Given the limitations of this model, binder incorporation and mechanical manipulation may affect particle occupancy and volumetric stability. Reducing graft manipulation may enhance space maintenance and facilitate bone regeneration.

title: Experience-based recommendations for the diagnosis and management of early-stage nail unit melanoma.
abstract: Background Nail unit melanoma (NUM) is a distinct form of melanoma that most often arises from the nail matrix. No recommendations as to the management of nail melanoma, particularly of early-stage melanoma (in situ, stage IA, IB), exist. Objectives To provide practical, experience-based recommendations for the diagnosis, differential diagnosis and management of early-stage NUM, developed by an international expert panel. Methods Based on clinical and histopathological experience and an extensive literature search, the authors present recommendations for the management of patients with lesions suspicious for NUM. Results Clinically, most cases present as a longitudinal pigmented band in an adult nail. It represents 1.5-2.5% of all melanomas in Caucasians but up to 50% in Black patients. Considering that the nail unit surface area accounts for less than 1% of the total body surface, the nail matrix can be regarded as a hotspot for melanoma development. Early diagnosis is critical, as treatment at the in situ or minimally invasive stage is associated with high cure rates. While dermoscopy is a useful diagnostic aid, nail matrix biopsy with histopathology remains the gold standard. Laboratory tests and standard imaging studies are not diagnostic; however, they may assist in surgical planning for advanced cases. Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Wide local excision is recommended for early-stage disease, with specific margins (6 mm for standard lesions; 10 mm in the presence of the Hutchinson sign). Amputation is generally reserved for thicker tumours (>1 mm). A 10-year follow-up period is recommended to monitor for potential recurrence. Conclusions Early diagnosis and treatment of nail unit melanoma at the in situ or minimally invasive stage (IA/IB) are associated with high cure rates. In contrast, advanced disease with deep invasion or metastasis carries a poor prognosis-therefore, timely recognition and intervention are essential to optimize outcomes.

title: Health Economic & Implementation Determinants of Prehospital Stroke Triage Tools: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Effective prehospital stroke triage enables faster treatment and better patient outcomes. Although prehospital triage innovations are rapidly emerging, evidence regarding the balance between costs and benefits as well as implementation issues remains limited. This review aims to synthesise published evidence on health economics and implementation determinants of prehospital triage tools for acute suspected ischaemic stroke patients. A systematic search was conducted across five databases (CINAHL, Cochrane, EMBASE, PubMed, and Web of Science) between 1995 and 2025. Results were reported narratively, and reporting quality was assessed using CHEERS, STROBE-simulation, COREQ, CONSORT, SQUIRE, and GRAMMS. Included were empirical studies of EMS-operated prehospital triage innovations for acute suspected stroke patients. The main outcome measures were health economic outcomes (e.g., ICER) and system-level implementation determinants (CFIR constructs). From 6491 screened studies, thirty-one were included: thirteen studies included health economic outcomes and eighteen reported implementation determinants. Prehospital triage tools assessed were: MSU (n = 14), telemedicine (n = 13), clinimetrics (n = 1), prehospital MRI (n = 1), biomarkers (n = 1), and an AI-based microwave tool (n = 1). Most studies (68%) were of high reporting quality. Positive results regarding cost-effectiveness were reported (n = 11), including cost-savings (n = 1), as well as implementation determinants (n = 11). However, evidence on sustained implementation was limited. Barriers included innovation design, complexity, workflow compatibility, work and IT infrastructure, and costs. Included studies suggest most prehospital stroke triage tools are cost-effective, but implementation remains largely context-dependent. Barriers, including innovation complexity, role delineation, workflow fit, design, and costs, highlight the need for future studies to integrate health economics into an implementation science framework alongside clinical outcomes.

title: When the Algorithm Speaks First: Trust, Reliance and the Reconstruction of Clinical Metacognition.
abstract: Aims of the journal addressed This paper addresses three of the aims of the Journal: clinical decision making, health philosophy and person-centred healthcare. Retinal imaging serves as the analytic case. The question at issue, what epistemic attitude a clinician may properly hold towards an algorithmic output issued for an individual patient, arises in every discipline and every health system in which such systems are deployed, and the argument is tested throughout against systems that read no images. Rationale, aims and objectives Diagnostic artificial intelligence increasingly delivers a conclusion before the clinician has formed one, and medical education has responded by adding modules on the critical appraisal of algorithmic output. Such curricula rest upon two unsound foundations: they extend a form of metacognitive instruction shown not to improve diagnostic accuracy and they ask clinicians to cultivate an attitude whose defining feature is the relaxation of validation. This paper establishes what epistemic attitude a clinician may hold towards an algorithmic output and derives the form that clinical metacognition must take in consequence. Methods Conceptual analysis, drawing upon the philosophy of trust and epistemic dependence, the cognitive science of clinical reasoning and empirical studies of artificial intelligence in clinical practice. Retinal medicine serves as the analytic case, chosen because it is the domain in which the position under contest is strongest; the argument is tested throughout against systems that process no images. Results Trust and reliance are distinct attitudes. On the account adopted here, to trust a medical algorithm is to rely upon it while relaxing the monitoring of the conditions that make it reliable; trust is reliance from which validation has been withdrawn. Regulatory clearance, institutional adoption and published performance supply legitimate grounds for trusting the assemblage that produces a system, yet none of them, singly or together, warrants reliance upon its output for an individual patient. Three asymmetries separate algorithmic from human epistemic dependence: the algorithm can be neither interrogated nor held to account; its errors fall on whole classes of patients at once; and its warrant holds of a population while the decision is owed to a person. The metacognition this situation demands is knowledge, not disposition, and stands untouched by the evidence against generic metacognitive instruction. Conclusions Clinical metacognition requires reconstruction around three competences: calibrated reliance, awareness of distributed epistemic labour, and vigilance towards confidence-masked uncertainty. Each is content-dependent, teachable and assessable. Since none can be exercised where institutions supply neither the means of interrogation nor the time it takes, the reform of education and the reform of clinical governance are, in this respect, a single undertaking.

Such curricula rest upon two unsound foundations: they extend a form of metacognitive instruction shown not to improve diagnostic accuracy and they ask clinicians to cultivate an attitude whose defining feature is the relaxation of validation. This paper establishes what epistemic attitude a clinician may hold towards an algorithmic output and derives the form that clinical metacognition must take in consequence.

Methods

Conceptual analysis, drawing upon the philosophy of trust and epistemic dependence, the cognitive science of clinical reasoning and empirical studies of artificial intelligence in clinical practice. Retinal medicine serves as the analytic case, chosen because it is the domain in which the position under contest is strongest; the argument is tested throughout against systems that process no images.

Results

Trust and reliance are distinct attitudes. On the account adopted here, to trust a medical algorithm is to rely upon it while relaxing the monitoring of the conditions that make it reliable; trust is reliance from which validation has been withdrawn. Regulatory clearance, institutional adoption and published performance supply legitimate grounds for trusting the assemblage that produces a system, yet none of them, singly or together, warrants reliance upon its output for an individual patient. Three asymmetries separate algorithmic from human epistemic dependence: the algorithm can be neither interrogated nor held to account; its errors fall on whole classes of patients at once; and its warrant holds of a population while the decision is owed to a person. The metacognition this situation demands is knowledge, not disposition, and stands untouched by the evidence against generic metacognitive instruction.

Conclusions

Clinical metacognition requires reconstruction around three competences: calibrated reliance, awareness of distributed epistemic labour, and vigilance towards confidence-masked uncertainty. Each is content-dependent, teachable and assessable. Since none can be exercised where institutions supply neither the means of interrogation nor the time it takes, the reform of education and the reform of clinical governance are, in this respect, a single undertaking.

title: Organ Wet Mount (Squash) Preparations in Fish Pathology: An Underused, Rapid and Low-Cost Tool for Tissue-Level Diagnosis During Necropsy.
abstract: Rapid, practical diagnostic approaches are essential for effective fish health management, yet cytological wet mount assessment of internal organs remains underused and inconsistently described in peer-reviewed aquatic veterinary literature. Organ wet mount (squash preparation) cytology offers a simple, low-cost method for immediate evaluation of fresh tissues. Unlike impression smears and aspirates, in which cells are assessed largely in isolation, squash preparations retain structural relationships within the tissue, providing tissue-level information at the point of examination that would otherwise await histopathology. The technique is widely applicable and requires minimal equipment, but guidance on its application beyond gill, skin, and fin samples is limited. A survey of fish health professionals confirmed that internal organ preparations are used less than external wet mounts. This review outlines the use of organ squash preparations during fish necropsy, emphasising technique, interpretation, and recognition of common findings rather than a comprehensive overview of disease. Key limitations, such as post-mortem changes, are discussed, as is the role of targeted special stains and follow-up diagnostics. Greater awareness and more consistent use of organ squash cytology have the potential to improve early detection of disease and support more targeted diagnostic decision-making in fish health investigations.

title: Geographic Distribution of Adult Salmon Enteritis (ASE), Enterocytozoon schreckii, and Ceratonova shasta in Chinook Salmon Oncorhynchus tshawytscha (Walbaum, 1792) in Select Oregon and Washington State Hatcheries and Expanded Histopathologic Description of ASE.
abstract: Adult salmon enteritis (ASE) is a severe intestinal disease affecting spring Chinook Salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) in the Pacific Northwest. ASE is strongly associated with prespawn mortality (PSM), a critical concern for endangered populations and continued Chinook Salmon management. This study characterizes the geographic distribution of ASE across Oregon and Washington watersheds, examines its association with two common parasites (Ceratonova shasta and Enterocytozoon schreckii), and provides detailed histopathological characterization of the disease. We examined intestinal tissues from 259 adult spring Chinook Salmon collected from multiple hatcheries across the Columbia River Basin and Puget Sound between 2022 and 2025 using routine histopathology, specific histochemical stains, and immunohistochemistry. ASE was highly prevalent in all Columbia Basin populations, with chronic ulcerative and necrotizing enteritis, but was absent in Puget Sound populations. C. shasta prevalence was high in most Columbia Basin locations (10%-100%), while E. schreckii prevalence was more variable (0%-67%). Consistent histopathological findings of ASE included ≥ 10% mucosal ulceration, mixed inflammation expanding the lamina propria and extending into surrounding intestinal layers, and dissolution of the stratum granulosum. In chronic ASE lesions, we further characterized granulation tissue formation. Cold water holding of spawning adults appears to slow disease progression and reduce PSM without preventing ASE development. These findings demonstrate that ASE is a geographically restricted disease of the Columbia Basin that may have associations with diverse environmental exposures including water temperature and pathogens.

title: Integrating Plain 2D Ultrasound and Clinical Data for Identification of At-Risk MASH: A Multicenter Proof of Concept Study.
abstract: Background Identifying people with at-risk metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a major challenge. We aimed to use deep learning to develop a convolutional neural network (CNN) model to facilitate the detection of at-risk MASH. Methods A multi-center cohort study was conducted across five tertiary hospitals in Japan and China. Clinical data and conventional ultrasound images were retrospectively collected. Organ segmentation using YOLO version 11 with quality control was performed, followed by creation of an EfficientNet-B6 CNN regression model, with image-level predictions averaged per patient, to estimate FAST and AGILE 3+ risk categories. Model performance was assessed using agreement across clinically relevant rule-out and rule-in thresholds, R 2 , root mean squared error (RMSE), and area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC). Results The final dataset comprised 416 patients for training (7643 images), 139 for internal validation (2463 images), and 154 for external testing (3539 images). The CNN model demonstrated good agreement with FAST (R 2 = 0.684; RMSE = 0.131; category agreement = 0.71) and moderate agreement with AGILE 3+ (R 2 = 0.445; RMSE = 0.1964; category agreement = 0.63). For FAST, AUROC was 0.974 (95% CI 0.947-0.993) for 0.35 and 0.932 (95% CI 0.884-0.969) for the 0.67 cut-off. For AGILE 3+, AUROC was 0.908 (95% CI 0.854-0.950) for 0.451 and 0.902 (95% CI 0.839-0.953) for the 0.679 cut-off. Conclusion The CNN model applied to clinical ultrasound images can approximate the accuracy of VCTE-based composite risk scores for detecting at-risk MASH. This may support the detection of at-risk MASH in settings with limited access to transient elastography.

title: Longitudinal Gut Microbiota Changes in Mouse Models of Chronic Colitis, Colitis-Associated Cancer, and Chemotherapy-Induced Diarrhea.
abstract: Background Gut microbiota contributes to intestinal pathologies, but microbial and metabolic differences distinguishing inflammation-associated tumorigenesis from chronic colitis remain unclear. This study mapped stage-dependent microbiota dynamics and metabolic perturbations across three independent mouse models: chronic ulcerative colitis (CUC), AOM/DSS-induced colitis-associated cancer (CAC), and chemotherapy-induced diarrhea (CID). Methods CUC, CAC, and CID were induced by cyclic DSS, AOM/DSS, and CPT-11, respectively. Disease progression was monitored via endoscopy, histopathology, and Disease Activity Index. Gut microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing across three stages (R01-R03); metabolic and inflammatory changes were assessed by RT-qPCR and metabolite assays. Mediation analysis was used to explore whether the associations between microbial abundance and host metabolic/inflammatory markers were statistically consistent with an indirect pathway. Results CID showed distinct acute transient injury and a unique microbiota structure separate from CUC/CAC. In CUC and CAC, microbiota restructured stage-dependently: beneficial genera (Akkermansia) declined, while pathobionts (norank_o_Clostridia_UCG-014) increased. CAC showed upregulation of glycolysis genes (HK2, PKM2, LDHA, Glut1) together with elevated colonic lactate concentrations, and elevated colonic concentrations of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-17A and IL-22, indicating distinct colonic metabolic and inflammatory changes associated with gut dysbiosis. Mediation analysis showed that norank_o__Clostridia_UCG-014 showed consistently positive indirect effects, irrespective of the glycolytic enzyme and lactate enantiomer examined; and Allobaculum had a consistently positive indirect effect on both IL-17A and IL-22. Conclusion These findings reveal distinct stage-specific microbial and metabolic signatures distinguishing AOM/DSS tumor-bearing mice from nonneoplastic chronic colitis and acute chemotherapy intestinal injury.

title: Impact of AI-Assisted Endoscopy on Secondary Review and Referral Decisions in Gastric Cancer Screening: A Multicenter Real-World Study.
abstract: Objectives Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted endoscopy may support gastric cancer screening, but its impact on structured secondary human review remains unclear. We evaluated secondary review modifications and referral decisions before and after AI implementation. Methods This retrospective multicenter study included 5013 screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy examinations performed before (n = 2021) and after (n = 2992) AI implementation. The primary outcome was secondary review modifications. Secondary outcomes included referral for further diagnostic evaluation. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, Helicobacter pylori eradication status, prior-year endoscopy, and endoscopist experience were performed. Interaction analyses according to endoscopist experience and inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses were conducted. No external reference standard was available to verify secondary-review modifications or referral decisions. Results Secondary review modifications increased from 1.2% in the pre-AI period to 3.7% in the AI period (p < 0.01). A significant interaction was observed between AI implementation and endoscopist experience (p for interaction < 0.01), with increased modifications primarily among nonexpert endoscopists. Cancer-related modifications remained uncommon but increased after AI implementation (0.6% vs. 0.2%, p = 0.04). Referral rates decreased from 4.9% to 2.8% (p < 0.01), and AI implementation was independently associated with lower odds of referral (adjusted OR = 0.53; 95% confidence interval = 0.36-0.77). Conclusions AI-assisted endoscopy was associated with lower referral rates; however, secondary review modifications persisted after AI implementation, particularly among nonexpert endoscopists. These findings describe workflow changes and do not establish the clinical validity of the modifications or the appropriateness of referral decisions.

title: Metaplasia and the Origins of Gastric Cancer-Implications for Screening and Surveillance.
abstract: Gastric intestinal metaplasia (IM) is a key step in the development of intestinal-type gastric cancer (GC) and a checkpoint for preventive strategies. The risk of progression to GC is highest for incomplete IM and extensive severe IM as classified by scoring systems such as operative link on gastric intestinal metaplasia (OLGIM) assessment, whereas the majority with mild or focal IM do not progress. Its pathogenesis is characterized by Helicobacter pylori-triggered chronic inflammation driving epithelial lineage reprogramming and CDX1/2 activation. IM clones develop and acquire early driver mutations (TP53, APC, and FBXW7), 8q/MYC gains, telomere attrition, and promoter hypermethylation, establishing a precancerous field, from which further evolution to dysplasia and cancer may occur. Recent preliminary data have suggested the possibility of reversing IM by MEK inhibition to induce mucosal reprogramming. Clinical management centers on H. pylori eradication, surveillance by high-quality endoscopy and guided by risk stratification using OLGIM or endoscopic grading of gastric intestinal metaplasia (EGGIM). Future work should prospectively validate tissue and blood biomarkers, integrate image-based risk scores into routine care, and test antiprogression and field-modifying therapies in randomized trials. In conclusion, IM is an actionable checkpoint for cancer interception, and its finding in a patient should prompt the consideration of surveillance and preventive strategies to avert progression to GC.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ultrasound for Sarcopenia Assessment: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Background Muscle ultrasound offers a portable, non-invasive, and cost-effective option for sarcopenia assessment, but operator dependency limits its standardization. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help automate and improve ultrasound-based muscle evaluation. This scoping review aims to map the current landscape of AI-assisted ultrasound for sarcopenia assessment, including research trends, methods, clinical uses and performance, and to suggest future work. Methods Following Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines and the PRISMA-ScR checklist, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, ProQuest, CNKI, WanFang Data, Yiigle, VIP, and Sinomed up to July 25, 2026. Two researchers independently selected studies and extracted data. Results Thirty studies were included. This field is developing rapidly, with 76.7% of studies published in the last 3 years, primarily from Spain and China. Model development and validation studies (43.3%) were most common. U-Net and its variants were the predominant AI architectures, mainly for image segmentation. B-mode ultrasound with high-frequency linear probes was frequently used. The rectus femoris was the most assessed muscle for sarcopenia (73.3%). AI-integrated models for sarcopenia diagnosis achieved AUCs of 0.640-0.950. Reported Dice coefficients for muscle segmentation ranged from 0.73 to 0.99. In-house datasets were used in 66.7% of the studies, and global classification labels were the most frequent annotation strategy (46.7%). Conclusions AI-assisted ultrasound shows potential for objective and scalable sarcopenia assessment but remains early-stage. Operator dependency in image acquisition has not been fully resolved. Further investigation should determine the added value of integrating multimodal imaging, combining diverse AI techniques, and evaluating multiple muscle groups. Future efforts should deepen image-processing strategies to extract clinically relevant features and facilitate standardized, scalable implementation in clinical practice.

title: Opportunistic Screening for Bone Demineralization by Whole Body CT in a Red-Handed Howler Monkey (Alouatta belzebul) Under Human Care.
abstract: An eight-year-old male red-handed howler monkey (Alouatta belzebul) underwent whole-body computed tomography for gastrointestinal signs. Quantitative CT of the lumbar vertebrae opportunistically revealed severe bone hypoattenuation, demineralization, and deteriorated trabecular architecture. This incidental diagnosis of metabolic bone disease was directly attributed to chronic inadequate management conditions, specifically a severely imbalanced diet and insufficient sunlight exposure in captivity.

title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis in Rhesus Macaque (Macaca mulatta): A Case Report.
abstract: Pulmonary tuberculosis caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTC) was diagnosed in a 6-year-old female rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) presented with a three-month history of intermittent coughing, dyspnea, weight loss, and inappetence. Hematological evaluation revealed moderate regenerative anemia and neutrophilic leukocytosis, while the thoracic radiography demonstrated a diffuse nodular interstitial pulmonary pattern consistent with tuberculosis. The diagnosis was confirmed by IS6110-targeted PCR. This case underscores the utility of combining radiographic and molecular diagnostic approaches for the early confirmation of tuberculosis in nonhuman primates and highlights its important zoonotic implications.

title: Genetic landscape of a neonatal hypogonadotropic hypogonadism series: Novel variants and phenotypic spectrum.
abstract: To describe clinical presentation and genetic findings in a cohort of infants with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) diagnosed before 2 years of age. From a large cohort of patients who underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS) for CHH between 2019 and 2025, we identified all patients tested at ≤2 years of age. Genetic analysis consisted of a targeted CHH gene panel, followed by a CPHD-NGS panel. In one remaining patient with neurodevelopmental defects, whole-exome sequencing was performed. Phenotypic data were collected through the GENHYPOPIT registry. Twelve male infants (1.5% of the total cohort) met the inclusion criteria; one additional patient via familial screening was included, for a total of 13 patients. All had micropenis; four had associated cryptorchidism (bilateral in half of cases). CHH was biologically confirmed during mini-puberty in 10 infants, at a median age of 6.8 weeks. Seven of these 10 infants received gonadotropin therapy, at an average of 4.1 months. MRI revealed bilateral olfactory bulb agenesis in five cases. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in 7 of 12 patients (58%), involving TACR3 (n = 2), ANOS1, FGFR1 (including two novel variants), SOX10, GLI2 (through the CPHD panel), and SOX11 (identified by exome sequencing). A genetic cause was identified in 58% of cases, a diagnostic yield higher than reported in pubertal cohorts. Early genetic diagnosis allowed anticipatory monitoring for syndromic manifestations and associated pituitary deficiencies-particularly relevant for FGFR1 and GLI2 variant carriers at risk of CPHD. Our findings support the inclusion of GLI2 and SOX11 in targeted HH gene panels.

title: Characterizing bone metastases and skeletal-related events in patients with well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms utilizing <sup>68</sup>Gallium-DOTATATE positron emission tomography.
abstract: Tumors of neuroendocrine origin are a heterogenous group of related neoplasms which can arise from anywhere in the body. Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) are categorized by site of origin, differentiation status and grade (Ki-67 expression and/or mitotic rate), with significant prognostic variability accordingly. Historically, the prevalence of bone metastasis is reported to be 6%-12% based on "first generation" (i.e., 111 Indium pentetreotide [Octreoscan®]) somatostatin receptor imaging (SSRI). We conducted a retrospective cohort study including patients with well-differentiated NENs to determine the clinical and imaging characteristics of osseous metastases when evaluated with higher-sensitivity 68 Gallium-DOTATATE positron emission tomography (PET) scans, as well as determining fracture prevalence in selected sub-cohorts. We also developed a risk score analysis to assess risk of fracture in this cohort. Four hundred twenty-four patients were identified for inclusion. The median age was 61 years. Most patients were asymptomatic (64%), had sclerotic lesions (77%), Krenning 4 (71%), and had >3 sites (69%) of osseous disease. A high proportion of patients had osseous metastases at sites with high risk for fracture, including vertebra (82%), pelvis (63%), and peri-trochanteric femur (34%). Fifty-seven patients (13%) in the entire cohort suffered a fracture. Fracture prevalence was significantly lower in small bowel neuroendocrine tumors (NETs, 7%) and Grades 1 and 2 disease (8% and 9%, respectively), with higher prevalence in pancreatic NETs, paragangliomas/pheochromocytomas, lung carcinoid, and Grade 3 disease (≥20% for each; p-values <.05). Our study showed that the rate of osseous metastatic disease approximates 20% in well-differentiated NENs. Most bone metastases are asymptomatic and the risk of fracture is variable based on the primary site of disease and tumor grade. Our novel risk score analysis for fracture was designed to assist clinician decision making as to management of bone metastasis in this patient population.

title: Metastasis of Invasive Ductal Carcinoma of the Breast to the Uterine Cervix 30 Years Post-Mastectomy: A Case Report.
abstract: Metastasis of invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast to the uterine cervix is rare, with only one report of a case occurring more than 20 years after the primary surgery. A 69-year-old woman presented with abnormal uterine cervical cytology (atypical glandular cells without tumor diathesis) 30 years after undergoing breast cancer surgery. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 38-mm cervical mass. Modified radical hysterectomy was performed. The resected specimen exhibited an immunohistochemical profile of GATA3(+)/mammaglobin(+)/PAX8(-), which definitively excluded primary cervical adenocarcinoma and confirmed the diagnosis of metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma. Crucially, although the primary tumor was hormone receptor-positive, cervical metastasis exhibited receptor conversion to HER2-positive status. This case underscores the importance of considering metastatic breast cancer in the differential diagnosis of cervical masses in breast cancer survivors regardless of the disease-free interval. This further highlights the necessity for receptor re-evaluation in metastatic lesions to guide appropriate targeted therapy.

title: Sex-Discordant Monochorionic Dizygotic Twins After Double Blastocyst Transfer: Blood Chimerism Demonstrated by Multimodal Genetic Testing.
abstract: A 38-year-old woman conceived after intracytoplasmic sperm injection and frozen-thawed double blastocyst transfer. First-trimester ultrasonography suggested monochorionic diamniotic twins, but discordant external genitalia were identified at 21 weeks of gestation. Delivery at 37 weeks resulted in phenotypically normal female and male infants. Placental histopathology confirmed monochorionic diamniotic placentation. Postnatal multimodal genetic evaluation, including G-banding, single nucleotide polymorphism array, and buccal cell X/Y fluorescence in situ hybridization, demonstrated mixed 46,XX/46,XY cell lines in peripheral blood, consistent with predominantly blood-limited chimerism. Single nucleotide polymorphism array analysis demonstrated admixture of two independently derived genomes and findings inconsistent with a primary dispermic mechanism. These results supported a diagnosis of monochorionic dizygotic twinning with predominantly blood chimerism, most likely reflecting intertwin cell exchange. This case highlights the value of integrating tissue-specific genetic findings with postnatal phenotypic and clinical assessment to interpret predominantly blood-limited chimerism in MCDZ twins.
